topic.title: Why a tax-free allowance that never moves takes more of a UK pay rise each year

title: UK Budget week: how a frozen £12,570 allowance quietly raises your tax
description: The Personal Allowance is £12,570 this tax year and the basic rate is 20%. If pay rises with prices at an assumed 3% a year for 5 years and the allowance stays put, more of the same real pay is taxed. This is fiscal drag, explained in Budget week, with no prediction of what the Budget will change. England, Wales and Northern Ireland rates; Scotland differs. Data: GOV.UK. Speak to a licensed financial adviser in your country before making financial decisions. Illustrative only. Not financial advice.

lines.text: Your tax-free £12,570 never moves. So why does your tax go up?
With a UK Budget coming, here's the part that hits every payslip. Up to £12,570, you pay no income tax.
Above it, the basic rate takes 20% of every extra pound.
Say your pay of £30,000 rises with prices, an assumed 3% a year. In 5 years, it's £34,778.
But if the allowance stays at £12,570, it falls behind. Kept up with prices, it would reach £14,572.
So more of the same real pay gets taxed. That's fiscal drag.
On Budget day, watch the thresholds, not just the rates.
